Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Egypt predominantly use paper-based patient records, with handwritten registers for clinical data like history, diagnosis, and treatment. A 2014 WHO-EMRO study in Alexandria PHC units showed parallel paper and early e-records, but paper had higher completeness; e-records varied widely by unit and were incomplete (EMRO study). Recent reports (2024-2026) indicate only 314 hospitals have EMRs, with public/rural lagging due to infrastructure limits (Arxiv paper). DHIS2 launched nationally in 2026 with pilots in select primary facilities for emergencies/refugees (nutrition screening in 16 sites), but not routine patient care at most rural clinics (DHIS2.org). National Digital Health Strategy 2025-2029 aims for ecosystem-wide digitalisation, but rural point-of-service remains paper-default. Barriers: poor connectivity, training gaps, resource scarcity in rural areas. Gap: Ambitious policies contrast with rural reality of paper dominance and pilot-only digital use.

revision_notes: Cited sources were fetched and are relevant but dated (2014 study; DHIS2 2026 launch note on emergency/refugee use only) and, taken alone, understate recent progress. Fresh search found authoritative, dated evidence (Ahram Online, 20 April 2026; Egypt Healthcare Authority official site, 19 August 2024; Regtech Africa, 20 June 2025) that Universal Health Insurance System (UHIS) Phase I has fully digitised primary healthcare facilities (285 primary care units/centres, including rural facilities) across six governorates (Port Said, Ismailia, Luxor, South Sinai, Suez, Aswan), with 6+ million electronic health records created. This is stronger than 'entirely paper' but coverage is confined to Phase I governorates (roughly a fifth of the country), with Phase II only beginning trial rollout in Minya in April 2026 and most other governorates' rural clinics still reliant on paper per the original cited sources. Recalculated to code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), reflecting a genuine but partial and geographically uneven digital footprint rather than the previously stated 'entirely paper'. Not a top-of-scale change, so no escalation required.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Egypt present a mixed but improving picture of digital data capture. Under the Universal Health Insurance System (UHIS), primary care units and centres in the six Phase I governorates (Port Said, Ismailia, Luxor, South Sinai, Suez and Aswan) - which include many rural and village facilities - have been fully digitised, with electronic health records, e-prescriptions and unit-level digital archiving now standard. Phase II, beginning trial operations in Minya in April 2026 and later extending to Matrouh, Damietta, Kafr El-Sheikh and North Sinai, is expected to extend similar digitisation to a further five governorates covering over 12 million citizens. Outside UHIS-covered governorates, rural clinics still rely predominantly on paper registers, and DHIS2, launched nationally in January 2026, is so far used mainly for emergency and refugee health screening rather than routine primary care data capture. Overall, digital capture at rural clinics is present and growing but remains partial rather than the national norm.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Egypt has national digital transformation initiatives in law enforcement, including the Digital Justice Platform by Egabi that starts with complaint registration and police record issuance at stations, and a unified law enforcement system integrating criminal cases.Egabi Digital Justice Platform, SIS Egypt. However, EFHR reports (2021) indicate police stations, especially outside Cairo/Alexandria (i.e., rural), often lack technology, with ~50% documents handwritten; arrest/investigation records sometimes paper-based depending on location.ECOI/IRB EFHR Report. No rural-specific digitalisation evidence found; paper predominant at rural stations with digital aggregation higher up, fitting score 2.

A December 2025 MCIT press release confirms the Public Prosecution's systems are now fully paperless and digitally integrated with 118 police departments for reporting and statistics, and a January 2026 news report describes new mobile technology centres extending criminal-record and civil-status services beyond fixed offices, part of the Haya Karima rural programme. However, the same MCIT release states the goal is to 'accelerate the full implementation of the law enforcement system digitally across all governorates', indicating the rollout is ongoing rather than complete, and the older EFHR-documented reliance on handwritten records outside Cairo/Alexandria remains the best available evidence specific to non-metropolitan stations. revised_comments: Digital data capture in Egyptian police stations, including rural ones, is expanding but remains incomplete. The Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Communications and Information Technology have rolled out an integrated Digital Justice Platform whose police-station module allows complaints and police records to be registered and issued electronically, feeding into the Public Prosecution's now fully paperless case-management system, with the collaboration extended to 118 police departments by late 2025. Mobile technology centres, including units delivered in January 2026 for criminal-record and civil-status services, are being extended to reach citizens outside main urban centres as part of the broader Haya Karima rural development programme. Official statements describe plans to accelerate full digital implementation of the law enforcement system across all governorates, indicating the rollout is still in progress rather than complete, and independent reporting on stations outside Cairo and Alexandria continues to note substantial reliance on handwritten documentation. Rural police stations therefore combine growing digital record-keeping with continued predominant use of paper for day-to-day intake.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices and civil registration points in Egypt predominantly use paper-based forms for recording births and other vital events. Notifications are collected manually from health offices (some digitized via EBDRS since 2017 for ~4,571 offices, including rural via GPRS/3G) and sent as paper to local Civil Registry Offices, then compiled at governorate level where electronic data entry occurs before central processing WHO EMRO Questionnaire. Civil registry offices lack computers, scanners, internet, or other digital equipment—only paper is used WHO EMRO Questionnaire. Digital systems like EBDRS handle health notifications digitally at point-of-care and notify civil registry electronically, but registration at registry remains paper/manual African Union EBDRS. Recent advances (2024-2026) focus on urban kiosks/machines for certificate issuance and biometric apps for online services, with no evidence of rural rollout Ahram Online. Key barriers: poor ICT infrastructure in villages, no mobile registration units, inadequate budgets. National ambition (Egypt Vision 2030) pushes digital gov, but rural point-of-service lags, relying on aggregation/transcription—score 2 reflects some digital upstream but predominant paper at rural registries.

A October 2025 news report (elfagr.org) confirms the Ministry of Interior's civil status sector has extended its 'smart registry' pilot - previously operating only in Cairo for around four years - to Minya governorate, including rural/Upper Egypt centres (Bani Mazar, Shalabi), for digital issuance of birth, marriage and death certificates, with further national rollout planned. This is the first direct evidence of digital capture reaching a rural civil registry setting. Coverage remains limited to a small number of pilot governorates, so most rural registry offices continue to rely on manual paper intake. Recalculated to code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), matching the original comment's own conclusion. Not a top-of-scale change.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Egypt are in the early stages of digitisation. Since 2017, the Electronic Birth and Death Registration System (EBDRS) has digitised birth and death notifications at around 4,571 health offices nationwide, including rural facilities, which then transmit data electronically to civil registry offices for compilation. At the civil registry office itself, a 'smart registry' pilot for issuing birth, marriage and death certificates, first introduced in Cairo some four years earlier, has since October 2025 been extended to Minya governorate - including rural, Upper Egypt centres such as Bani Mazar and Shalabi - with further rollout planned nationally as part of the Ministry of Interior's civil status modernisation programme. Village-level notary and documentation offices are also being newly opened under the Decent Life (Haya Karima) rural development initiative. Outside these pilot areas, rural registry offices continue to rely on manual paper intake, with electronic data entry occurring mainly at governorate level rather than at the point of registration. Rural civil registration therefore combines a predominantly paper-based process with a small but growing number of digitised offices.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Egypt has an EMIS system integrated with national dashboards for decision-making, with recent (2025) EMIS-linked daily attendance monitoring achieving >80% attendance nationwide, including rural areas World Education Blog. 36,878/42,931 schools meet smart school criteria, but primary schools average 95 students/device, indicating limited digital tools in rural primaries UNESCO IICBA. World Bank projects mention EMIS data use but no school-level collection details. No evidence of direct digital recording (e.g., tablets/apps) at rural primary schools for attendance/enrollment/grades; likely paper-based with later aggregation (pilots/digital in some). Rural infrastructure gaps affect data reliability. Predominantly paper with some digital/pilots.

revision_notes: The World Education Blog (GEM Report) source cited in the row was fetched and read in full; it is authoritative, being based on a CAPMAS-verified Ministry of Education dataset, and directly supports the existing assessment. It confirms that by the end of the 2024/25 academic year, national attendance rose above 80% via EMIS-linked monitoring, 36,878 of 42,931 schools meet 'smart school' criteria, and over 54,000 schools have reliable internet - but primary schools average 95 students per digital device (versus near 1:1 in secondary/TVET), and the source itself flags that infrastructure gaps particularly affect remote areas. A supplementary case study (Menoufia governorate, villages under the Decent Life programme) corroborates that digital tools (tablets, smart classrooms) exist only in pockets of rural primary education, with most instruction and record-keeping still paper-based. Confirmed at code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); no change to the Value Code.
revised_comments: Digital data capture in Egyptian rural primary schools remains predominantly paper-based with a growing but still limited digital layer. Nationally, 36,878 of 42,931 schools meet 'smart school' criteria and more than 54,000 schools have reliable internet connectivity, and EMIS-linked daily attendance monitoring helped raise nationwide attendance above 80% by the end of the 2024/25 academic year, according to the Ministry of Education and Technical Education's CAPMAS-verified dataset. However, primary schools average 95 students per shared digital device, compared to close to one-to-one ratios in secondary and technical education, indicating that most day-to-day record-keeping and attendance-taking in rural primary classrooms is still done on paper before being aggregated into EMIS. Targeted programmes, such as tablet provision to Upper Egypt community schools and Decent Life (Haya Karima) smart-classroom pilots in villages such as Manshat Sultan (Menoufia), demonstrate pockets of direct digital capture, but these remain localised rather than the rural norm. Overall, rural primary schools sit between predominantly paper practice and emerging digital capture.
